headline: Eight US states sue OpenAI over ChatGPT safety for kids
dek: Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho and Montana accuse the company of misleading parents, per CNBC and The Verge.

s2.label: What happened
s2.title: Eight separate lawsuits
body: Eight US states sued OpenAI on Wednesday, accusing ChatGPT of being an unsafe product that harmed children and misled parents (CNBC, The Verge).
Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho and Montana each filed separately in state court (CNBC).

s3.label: How it works
s3.title: What the lawsuits claim
s3.body: These are the states' allegations, which OpenAI disputes. According to The Verge, they say it put profit over safety.

points.t: Violating state consumer-protection laws by failing to warn about the product's dangers (The Verge).
Presenting ChatGPT as safe for young people when it was allegedly dangerous to vulnerable users (The Verge).
Collecting data from minors without keeping them off the chatbot (The Verge).

s4.label: Why it matters
s4.title: What the states want
body: The states ask for civil penalties and for OpenAI to stop misleading the public about ChatGPT's safety. Some also seek deletion of data collected unlawfully (The Verge).
Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said OpenAI is hurting kids (CNBC).

items.t: It cites age-specific protections and parental controls, and wants to work with states (CNBC, The Verge).
It already faces wrongful-death suits filed by families (CNBC).
Florida's attorney general also sued the company in June (CNBC).

caption.hook: Eight US states sued OpenAI, accusing ChatGPT of harming children and misleading parents.
body: According to CNBC and The Verge, Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho and Montana filed separate suits. They allege violations of consumer-protection laws and data collection from minors. These are accusations, not yet decided in court.

The states seek civil penalties and an end to what they call misleading claims. OpenAI says it has age-specific protections, such as parental controls and break reminders, and wants to work with states on rules for the whole industry.
caption.cta: Should AI companies be held to child-safety rules like other consumer products?
